solution:
Section 1.4 'Notable Scholars', in the paragraph on Voltaire (1694-1778), states verbatim: "Thus, it is said that Voltaire was the founder of modern historiography."

The chapter builds to that sentence: Voltaire "opined that along with objective truth and chronology of historical events considering social traditions, trade, economy, agriculture, etc. was also equally important in historiography. It gave rise to the thought that understanding all aspects of human life is important for history writing." The founding claim is therefore tied to Voltaire widening the scope of history to all aspects of human life, not to his method.

The three distractors are each described in the same section doing something the chapter does NOT call 'founding modern historiography': René Descartes "was the foremost among scholars who insisted on verifying the reliability of historical documents by critically examining them" (his rule from 'Discourse on the Method' is credited with impact on "the scientific method of research"); Leopold von Ranké is credited with the critical method of historical research and the primacy of original documents, and with greatly influencing "[h]istoriography of the nineteenth century"; Karl Marx is credited with a "new school of thought" and the class-struggle thesis.

One caution is worth stating plainly, because it cuts against what is usually taught: outside this textbook the title 'father/founder of modern (scientific) historiography' is most often given to Leopold von Ranké — option C — on the strength of his source-critical, archive-based method (the 'wie es eigentlich gewesen' tradition) and the Berlin seminar. A reader working from general knowledge of historiography would very plausibly pick C. This chapter does not make that claim: it credits Ranke only with the critical method and with influencing nineteenth-century historiography, and reserves the word 'founder' for Voltaire alone. Because the item is to be derived from this chapter's own words, the answer is A (Voltaire); C is the outside-the-book answer and is not supported by any sentence here.

Section 1.4, paragraph on Michel Foucault (1926-1984), states: "The French historian of the twentieth century, Michel Foucault brought forth a new concept in historiography. He, in his book, 'Archaeology of Knowledge', argued that the prevailing practice of arranging historical events in a chronological order is not right." The same paragraph reinforces it: "He called his method, 'the archaeology of knowledge'."

The distractors are excluded by the chapter's own attributions: Karl Marx's named work is "'Das Kapital', a treatise written by him"; Voltaire is given no book title in this chapter (only his original name, Francois-Marie Arouet, and his views); Lucien Febvre is not named anywhere in the chapter at all — the chapter refers to the Annales School collectively ("The Annales School was started by French historians") without naming its founders, so the Lucien Febvre option has no textual footing here. Unambiguous: B.
